explanation:
## The one new line

Everything about a write that differs from a read is one flag, so there
is one lookup:

```cpp
bool Cache::write(std::uint64_t addr) {
    const bool hit = access(addr);        // allocate, evict, count, all of it
    const Decoded d = decode(addr);
    const std::size_t base = d.index * ways_;
    for (std::size_t w = 0; w < ways_; ++w) {
        Line& line = lines_[base + w];
        if (line.valid && line.tag == d.tag) { line.dirty = true; break; }
    }
    return hit;
}
```

and inside `access`, where the victim is chosen:

```cpp
++evictions_;
if (lines_[base + victim].dirty) ++writebacks_;
```

followed by `line.dirty = false` on the line being filled. That last
assignment is easy to forget and it is what the test
`write 0 / read 100 / read 200` is for: the block that arrives at
`read 100` must not inherit the dirty bit of the block it replaced, or
the second eviction reports a writeback that never happened.

## Why write-back rather than write-through

A write-through cache sends every store to memory. It is simpler — no
dirty bit, no writeback on eviction — and it is what you want when two
caches have to agree with each other. Its cost is traffic: a loop that
writes the same cache line a thousand times sends a thousand stores.

Write-back sends one, when the line leaves. The sample shows it in four
lines: two writes to the same address produce exactly one writeback, and
only when the block is actually pushed out.

The counting rule that follows is the one this milestone is really
testing: **a writeback is caused by an eviction, not by a write.** A
program can write all day and cause no traffic at all if it stays inside
the cache, and it can cause a writeback long afterwards on an access to
a completely unrelated address.

## Write-allocate, and when it is wrong

Allocating on a write miss is the right default: a program that writes a
byte usually writes the rest of the line soon after, and the last test
case — writing four consecutive bytes of one block — shows one miss and
three hits.

It is wrong for a streaming write that will never be read: copying a
gigabyte, the allocate fetches a line from memory only to overwrite all
of it. That is why real machines have non-temporal stores, which write
round the cache rather than through it.
